utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem or what? I do notice, incidentally, that there is much more light than usual. It's either in the anticipation of all the wisdom that we expect to hear, but there is more light than usual here. So if it's -- provided it's not annoying you, we can carry on. It's not annoying me. Can we start or not? The transcript is rolling, or scrolling, so that means we can start. So, Madam Registrar -- one moment. Yes. Basically, because I was following on the main monitor, our laptops are -- seem to be switched off. The relative -- the monitor accompanying the laptops are switched on, but not the -- can we in the meantime proceed, not to waste time, using the main monitors, Mr. Jones and Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think what happened is everyone's computers got switched off when the lights went off. We've switched ours back on and rebooted, and so we're now okay, and I presume that probably that would work for Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be that we have to do that too. All right. Okay. But it's not a problem. There will only be a discrepancy in the lines when it comes to transcript. Otherwise, we should be able to -- out of range, it says, but ... Set monitor to ... I don't know if this is going to work, but ... All right. In the meantime, I'll start working, okay. Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oric. Please sit down. And appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning to my learned colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team as well. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: None?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing I wanted to tell you, that from the information I am receiving, the documents that were supposed to be handed over to your expert in Sarajevo have been handed over way back on the 25th, I think, of October. However, it seems that your expert gave the indication to Ms. Thompson that he might need more than the one month that you had told us. So if you can exert some pressure on him to try and stick to that month, I think that would be extremely useful. But the procedure and protocol that we laid out, to my knowledge, went -- everything went smoothly, ran smoothly, and I will have the final report soon, okay, when Ms. Thompson comes back. But I just wanted you to know about this. So let's bring the witness in. What happened to the electricity? Are we on the main electricity or are we on a -- what do you call it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, we don't have the transcript on the LiveNote. We don't have that. And that's because we have to put in a password which we don't have. I mean, it's -- they need to come over and put in the password, yes, key in the password.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To us, it's not creating problems, but if it creates problems to any of you, please let us know. There he is. Basically, we are here and we need ... Yes, Mr. Sacirovic. Good morning to you. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two things: If there are problems with interpretation at any time, please let us know immediately; and second is that you are still testifying pursuant to your solemn undertaking. Ms. Richardson will continue with her cross-examination. Ms. Richardson, please, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to members of the Defence team, and good morning, Mr. Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to go over, just briefly, with you this morning some information that you gave on examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Your Honour, at this time, I would ask that the witness be given Prosecution's Exhibit P458. And if I could have the usher's assistance in showing the witness B/C/S ERN number 0359310, and in the English it is page 5, and it continues on page 6 in the English version. And this is the date, December 5th, 1992. It's page 7 in the handwritten of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, yesterday you indicated when you were asked on examination-in-chief by Mr. Jones about whether or not you knew a Mr. Mahmut?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mahmut Jugovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Jugovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you indicate -- thank you, Your Honour. You indicated that you did not know him. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, it says here that, if you're looking at the B/C/S version, it states here that he resides in the department store. And you also indicated that you yourself was a refugee. Could you tell us whether or not refugees resided in the department store in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I stayed at this address. I stayed in some miners' cottages that are some 200 metres away from the department store.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is a problem with interpretation, because Ms. Richardson never suggested that you said that you had resided here. It's about Mahmut Jugovic. She is saying that according to this document, Mahmut Jugovic resided in Robna Kuca, that's the department store, and she is asking you whether you are aware that at any time, refugees were staying -- were living in the department store, not whether you lived there; whether refugees lived there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am aware of that. Not only in the department store, but virtually in all the buildings. There were refugees in all the buildings in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you yourself arrived in Srebrenica as a refugee, I take it, how did you locate a place to live? How did you go about finding a place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived from Pale on foot. The War Presidency told me that there was a room in an apartment available, or rather, it was like a bed-sitter that was available in the miners' cottages belonging to the lead mines, lead and zinc mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you say the War Presidency, you're talking about Hajrudin Avdic, the president?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so he told you this place was available and that you could live there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They put me up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did you live there with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I would direct your attention to the second part of this entry, what is in relation to the second part, page 7 of the English, and the B/C/S is 03593132. And it begins on page 7 and continues on page 8. I would like to ask you specifically about what is stated here in this entry. Now, the entry does mention that there is a dispute over a fitted carpet. When I say dispute, just take it to mean strictly what is being stated here, that a -- there has been a report filed about carpet being taken. And could you tell us if carpet, whether fitted or not, was something of -- a valuable commodity to refugees?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that I don't know what this is all about. I never knew Mahmut Jugovic and I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, we are very short on time today, so if you could listen to my questions carefully. I'm not asking whether or not you knew what it was about. My question was specifically regarding the possession of carpet by a refugee. My question is: Would this be considered something valuable to a refugee who had nothing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that question. Probably it did mean something to them, but whatever I said would merely be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And based on -- well, let me ask you this: Refugees came to Srebrenica. They didn't come with beds or any type of furniture wherein they could sleep, for them to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that carpet is something that would have been able to be placed on a floor to enable someone to sleep on it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In that sense. But otherwise, it is not really of any high value, in pecuniary terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But during those times, when there was very little -- when the refugees came to Srebrenica with very little, you would agree that a piece of carpet which they could use to sleep on would be very valuable to them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what sort of value a piece of carpet could constitute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something else, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I was about to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day, where does it --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It also states here that clothes and shoes -- clothes and shoes which were used for exchange for grain. Now, my question to you is: Did people in Srebrenica, the refugees and other people who lived there, frequently exchange goods with each other?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that I know nothing about this. This was not within the scope of my research.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question is: To your knowledge, having lived in Srebrenica for a lengthy period of time, if people, the people of Srebrenica, the refugees and others, exchanged goods among themselves. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such exchanges, but I assure you that I wasn't interested in them. I was busy doing other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they exchanged, when, and how, I assure you, I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you answered my question. Now, on that same page - it's page 8 of the English, and it's the same page of the B/C/S; it's page 9, and it's 03593132 - there is a reference here to a Dr. Ejub. Now, you testified that you spent a substantial amount of time in the hospital. Could you tell us if there was a Dr. Ejub in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions on this document. And Dr. Ejub is Ejub Alic; that would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know Ejub. He was of rather short stature, broad-shouldered, but I wouldn't like to make a mistake, so that's why I can't tell you for a fact that his last name was Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he did treat people as a doctor in the Srebrenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that you came to Srebrenica as a result of being called by the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you proceeded to conduct interviews. And I'd like to ask you about the interview that you conducted with Ahmo Tihic. Firstly, let me first determine this: In that interview, we saw you were carrying a weapon. Could you tell us, without -- we don't have that much time, so I won't show you the interview again, but I believe you can probably remember since you were shown yesterday. You had a weapon. Could you tell us what type of a weapon you carried?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where did you get it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: For how much, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought the weapon in early 1992, in Sabac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And from whom?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought it from some Serbs who had been on the Vukovar battlefront. I knew that there was a war going on there. I knew that there was a war to break out here. That's why I bought myself a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what kind of a weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a semi-automatic rifle of Chinese make.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when in 1992? Do you remember what month you purchased this weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have a licence to carry the weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Licences were not issued for such types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If, Madam Vidovic, if you think that the way he has answered this question could in any way expose him to criminal proceedings in his country now, please tell me and we'll go into private session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you that it would not, for several reasons. One of them is the statute of limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If at any time, Mr. Sacirovic, you are asked questions that if you answer, you could possibly incriminate yourself, you can ask us to exempt you from answering such questions. You do not have an automatic right to be -- to get such exemption.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. I apologise to you for interrupting you, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. This is an important matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, you stated that you carried this weapon with you when you visited the field, and you also stated that in that video that we saw of Ahmo Tihic, when you were interviewing him, that there was a video operator. Could you tell us if -- I believe his name is Gujic, and please correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. With Ahmo Tihic, there was cameraman Sabahudin Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was he the only cameraman that was part of the commission on gathering data on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did he also carry a weapon when you went into the field to speak with fighters and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many members of your team would routinely go into the field to interview civilians and fighters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of them. Edhem Vranjkovina, Sabahudin Gluhic, and I. From time to time, they would go on their own, if I was busy and if they were to film something that was close by. But for the most part, we functioned as a team.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did Mr. Vranjkovina carry a weapon as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what kind of weapon did he carry?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vranjkovina carried an automatic rifle which he was issued with in the police building. The weapon was in the police station even before the war, because he used to be an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you went into the field, and I believe you said most frequently it would be the three of you, so was anyone else accompanying you to the sites of the civilians and the fighters, other than the three of you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was nobody else in our team except for the three of us. Someone might have joined us in the field out of sheer curiosity. Otherwise, the three of us made up the team that was authorised to do the thing that we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how did you go about locating -- well, I'll rephrase the question. You testified that you would routinely go into the field a number of times and you went to different villages in the Srebrenica area. Could you explain to us how it was that you came about making a decision about where, meaning which village, which village to visit to take reports and information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, we did not make the selection. It was Mr. Avdic, president of the War Presidency, who made the selection, and then we merely implemented his assignment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he would tell you exactly where to go, what village to go to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he would tell you where the civilians and the fighters were located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told us what had to be done, and circumstances permitting, we did what we were required to do. If the circumstances were not permitting it, like if there was shelling going on or any active fighting, we would come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how often -- I'll rephrase the question. How did he go about telling you where to go? Was it in -- was it verbal, verbally, or was it in writing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would mostly do it in writing. He'd write down that we had to film factories, destroyed villages, and so on. And we would act upon these written documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, a number of the civilians you interviewed, we saw yesterday, were in the forest areas were in the forest areas. Could you tell us how it was you knew exactly what area they were located in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the information reached the president of the War Presidency, who would then inform us where we had to go. He would tell us that we had to reach a certain area, enter a wooded area, and interview these people. We would then go to the given village, where the locals were able to tell us where we had to go on further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I see. So the locals -- well, correct me if I'm wrong: The locals would tell you exactly where the people were located; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was for the most part. For example, if there was a village on the ground, such as Biljeg, where Ahmo Tihic was, the president of the Presidency would say, "There's a group up there at Biljeg. Go up and see if they're there." Because people would arrive in the village -- people would arrive in Srebrenica and provide information as to where those people were, in the woods and in camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And yourself and the other members of the team, were you familiar with the terrain of Srebrenica? Did you have any trouble finding the location of the people? Did you need a guide?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't need a guide because, you know what, Edhem Vranjkovina was born in those parts, precisely where we were filming those women. Sabahudin Gluhic was also born in the Srebrenica area and I wasn't born far. So that we knew all the villages. Mr. Vranjkovina had been a policeman and a hunter, and for him it was no problem to locate a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you arrived, for instance, at a certain place, Biljeg, I take it you -- Biljeg is a fairly large area? Would you describe it as such?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, it's a hill, like a mountain. And there are woods there. I can't tell you the surface area in square miles or kilometres, so I can't say exactly what the surface area is or how big it is. It's a wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you knew exactly what part of the woods to find Ahmo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Edhem Vranjkovina who knew that, because he was very familiar with that terrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And during the videotaping of, for instance, the video that we saw of Ahmo Tihic, could you tell us how it was -- well, first, tell us what type of video equipment that was used, and tell us how it was powered.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: A video camera was used. The owner was Sabahudin Gluhic. The batteries were powered in the post office, where there was a kind of improvised mini powerplant, and there was an accumulator there and that was used to fill the batteries for the camera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how many videotapes do you think you made over a period of 1992 and 1993 of civilians and fighters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many. Many tapes were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And those tapes were made in Srebrenica, as well as in the field?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both in Srebrenica and in the field, and they were all submitted to the president of the War Presidency for safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you also film events in Srebrenica, such as celebrations and other type of events, in 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various kinds of filming. When the UN forces came in, it was easier to breathe, and it was possible to organise something very simple, some kind of sports, games, and things like that. So we did film those kinds of events too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, getting back to the interview that you had with Ahmo Tihic, you mentioned yesterday that on the tape that was shown to us, you addressed Ahmo Tihic as the platoon commander, and you said that you chose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I know what the objection is. It wasn't Ahmo Tihic who was --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- platoon commander; it was another young man sitting next to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would guess that's what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You addressed one of the individuals during your interview of Ahmo Tihic as the platoon commander, which I take it is a very specific military title or position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You know what, when I would see someone who was dejected, who was depressed, I did this kind of automatically, mechanically, like: Oh, are you the platoon commander? He wasn't a platoon commander. You can see from the tape itself that he was a young man full of misery. He was lost, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, when you addressed him as platoon commander, he didn't correct you, did he? On the tape, we did not see him --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't correct me, because he probably wasn't even fully conscious of what I'd said. He was traumatised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Or he didn't correct you because you were correct; isn't that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not correct. He was no platoon commander. It was just something I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that you interviewed the fighters, and of course you interviewed them about what was going on on the front line. Do you recall that evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you received this information, you took it back to Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you gave this information to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, the president of the War Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, information about the camps -- yes. But as for notes of interviews with the fighters, I didn't write anything down; I simply handed in the videotapes. I didn't hand in any written notes in connection with the fighters at Biljeg, only the videotape, because there was no need, and I didn't have an order or an assignment to interview them. I interviewed them out of pure curiosity, asking whether they were being shelled, whether there were any attacks, and so on. Just like when you meet someone today, you ask them how they're doing, how their family is, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You also testified that you spent a substantial amount of time in the hospital interviewing the fighters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hospital, I didn't interview only fighters; I interviewed the wounded. I did not distinguish or have a mandate to distinguish between fighters and others. All those in the hospital were simply the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's what you termed them, as wounded, but you were, were you not, once you began interviewing this person, able to determine whether they had taken part in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would learn whether the man had been at a front line somewhere or at home or out in the fields. I wasn't given the assignment of interviewing wounded fighters in particular, but I collected information from all wounded, in order to learn the truth about what had happened, to find out where and how they had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But in addition to finding out how they were wounded, you also received information, did you not, about what the Serbs were engaged in, for example, shelling, use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I obtained such information from what side the shooting came, what kind of weapons were used and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And indeed, it was from that series of -- those series of interviews over a period of time you were able to confirm yesterday on examination-in-chief a number of the documents regarding the build-up of Serb artillery, where they were located, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Yesterday you were asked a series of questions about the build-up of Serb -- the Serb military in the area of Srebrenica and the Bratunac municipality. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you testified that one of the ways you learned about the information that had been shown to you and presented to you in documents was because you had interviewed fighters in the hospital, or the wounded in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I interviewed the wounded in hospital, and I had the most up-to-date information as to what kind of weapons had been used, the weapons that caused the wounding, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was based on information collected on the spot in hospital. That's how I learnt what kind of weapons the Serbs were using to target Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it this was very important information, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: At that time, the situation was very confused. It was critical.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, my question is -- I hate to interrupt you, but if you could answer my question. Was that information about what the Serbs were engaged in militarily important information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it was important information for all of -- for the organs in Srebrenica? And the organs, by that I mean the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you transferred this information to the War Presidency because it was important.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, you also testified that you received some of the information via a radio.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We heard that information on the Serbian radio. We used an improvised transistor radio, which the electricians made by taking out the motor-powering windscreen wipers on a car and then they would take something from a spinning wheel, a part from a spinning wheel, and this wheel would be used to generate electricity for the transistor radio. And we would listen to the broadcasts of Serbian Radio Bratunac. Sometimes in the afternoon or the evening, whenever they were transmitting their news broadcasts, and a group of us would gather around the transistor radio to hear what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where was this transistor radio located? What building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several people who had those transistor radios. They were just ordinary transistor radios, like the ones that every household has. And they would take it outside, into the park, and they would turn this wheel to power it, and people would gather around to listen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So with this transistor radio, were you only able to listen to what was broadcast publicly or were you also able to listen to what the Serbs were discussing, the different Serb units, among themselves?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It was just an ordinary transistor, where you would tune in to a particular station and then listen. You'd tune in to Serb Radio Bratunac. It wasn't a radio station of the kind you mean. They were just ordinary transistor radios, like the ones you can buy any day, anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the radio that you're -- the news that you heard, are you saying that it was in regards to the Serb build-up in the area? Was it military information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information included both military and the civilian information. Very often, they would say they were receiving reinforcements, probably in order to raise the morale of their men, saying that certain units had arrived from Serbia as reinforcements, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the times that you went into the field, you indicated that you carried a weapon and so did the other member of your team, just in case of attacks, I take it. Were you ever attacked or ambushed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, we were very cautious. If the situation was at all dangerous, we would delay the filming. We would postpone it. So there was never an occasion when we were in real danger. We were very careful about that. It was better to go back than to expose our lives to danger.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, my question was: Were you ever attacked? Did you ever have cause to use your weapon or the other person that you were with, against being attacked by Serbs, that is, of course?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to get back, just briefly, to --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never. We never had any occasion to use our weapons. We never ran into an ambush and had to use the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Getting back briefly to what you testified to yesterday about your appointment by the president of the War Presidency. I'd like to talk to you about the other people. I think you've already mentioned two, two others, who were cameramen. Was there also a female there working with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. In our team, there was no woman. There were just the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were -- your team, that is, the commission for collecting data on war crimes, was under the communication and information division of the War Presidency. It was a department within the War Presidency. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this department was supervised by Hamed Alic, the entire department?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the other individuals in the department of communication and information. Are you familiar with Ibrahim Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Ibrahim Becirovic, but I don't know what role he played.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that he operated -- that he operated a radio and that individuals seeking to contact members of their family in Tuzla and other areas were able to speak to them over this radio in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I know that Hamed Alic was in charge of that radio station, which was located in the Srebrenica post office in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So, well, did you have occasion to see Mr. Becirovic at all in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember him vaguely. I don't really know him very well. He is the brother of Ramiz Becirovic, and that's why I know who he is. But I don't really know him really well, and his role is something I really don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you don't know what he did in Srebrenica during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, other than the three members of your commission, were you aware of other members, individuals, who worked under Hamed Alic as part of the communication and information system, or department?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. The decision on my appointment was signed by the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. The service for communications and information was also subordinate to the War Presidency, but I always took the information I obtained to Mr. Avdic only.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm seeking to determine whether or not you were aware of other members working under the communication and information system supervised by Mr. Hamed Alic. So my question is: With respect to other people, other than those of your commission, were there other people being supervised by Hamed Alic under the department of communication and information service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated or testified that Mr. Hamed Alic maintained an office in the same building, the same floor, as you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Hamed Alic had his office in the municipal -- or rather, in the post office building - excuse me - whereas my office was in the municipal building. The distance between the post office and the municipal building is 400 or 500 metres. Hajrudin - excuse me - Hamed Alic did not have an office in the municipal building, but in the post office building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I misspoke. I do recall that you did say that he had an office in the PTT building. Now, it was Mr. Hajrudin Avdic who had an office in the municipal building, where you worked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the same floor. It was the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: On the second floor. Who else occupied the second floor, other than yourself and Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzemaludin Becirovic and Hamdija Fejzic were there quite often. I would drop by quite often, as well as my team, and that was the part of the municipal building that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you were often out of the office during the times that you were interviewing people in the field and in the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go to the office quite often, although I would not spend a full eight hours there. I would hand in my documentation over there and that would be our point of departure for me and my team when we would go out into the field. Therefore, although I spent most of my time out in the field, I also spent some time in the office. Whenever I was in town, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also spent some time when you were in town at the hospital, as you testified before, a substantial amount of time, I believe you stated.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As soon as I found out about the arrival of new wounded, I would go over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who else was in the PTT building with Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about Hamed Alic being there. Occasionally, I would go to visit Hamed Alic in the post office building, but I would go directly to his office, where the radio was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Srebrenica Territorial Defence also occupied that office, that building?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you run into Ramiz Beckovic [sic] or Osman Osmanovic in that building whenever you visited?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I saw Ramiz Becirovic in Opetci, in his hometown in Suceska, whereas for Ramiz, I never saw him at all. I wasn't aware of anyone -- or rather, I didn't know anyone who was there except for Hamed Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you're familiar with Ramiz Becirovic. Do you know what his role was in Srebrenica during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what his role was. I told you that I got to know Ramiz Becirovic when I went into the field in the month of August and it was in Opetci in Suceska, his native village. That was where I met him, in his house, because he hails from Opetci. We were going there to film a school that was destroyed by shelling in Kamenica, and that was how I got to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know Osman Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it you did not go to the PTT building very often?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go there from time to time, when necessary. I wasn't there every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you go once a week, twice a week, once a month?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes once fortnightly, once monthly, but I would not stay there for too long. Whenever I went there, I simply had to consult Hamed on a matter, and that would be the whole purpose of my visit to the post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during that time that you visited the post office, I take it this is not where the briefings that you said you attended with Mirzet Halilovic took place.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Those briefings that you testified to yesterday or the day before, that took place with Mr. Bogilovic and Mirzet Halilovic and yourself, took place in the building you worked in, the municipal building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the office of the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you about those meetings that you testified about. You testified that meetings were held and that during those meetings Mirzet Halilovic was present and you also brought his report. And that is Mirzet Halilovic being the commander of the military police. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during that -- how often would you say you attended briefings where Mirzet Halilovic was present, Mr. Bogilovic -- and Mr. Bogilovic

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite often. I already told you that Becir Bogilovic was wounded and he came to the municipal building but rarely. But Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic did come. Mirzet Halilovic was the chief of the military police, whereas Nurija Jusufovic was the commander of the civilian police. They delivered their reports to the president of the War Presidency, as did I. To be precise, I believe we had an exact time when we had to hand them over. That was at 9.00 in the morning. And then we would receive assignments, if any. If, for instance, my commission had to go somewhere, we would receive an order signed by the president, and the same probably went for Mr. Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic, either or both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're going to get back to those meetings in a moment. You said that Mr. Bogilovic was wounded. Can you tell us if you know how he was wounded, where? Where, not meaning the part of the body, but what area was he in when he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded in the leg. I cannot vouch whether it was the left or the right leg. I only know for a fact that he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I actually didn't mean the part of the body, but do you know how he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know how and where he was wounded. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And other than the function that he served on the War Presidency, do you know if he had any other function in Srebrenica, Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogilovic was a member of the War Presidency and chief of the civilian and military police in Srebrenica in the period from -- to 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat from which year, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters did not catch which period this -- it starts from. In other words, until 1993, but from which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as far as you know, he didn't carry out any other activities that were not related to those of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the fact that he administered the two police departments, civilian and military police, he was member of the War Presidency. He had under his jurisdiction the two commanders of the civilian and military police, Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you see an order where Mr. Becirovic was made the chief of the military police, subordinating Mirzet Halilovic to him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was an order, or rather, a decision by the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, whereby Becir Becirovic was appointed chief of the civilian and military police in Srebrenica. I saw the decision with my own eyes. It was appended, along with all the other decisions, on the announcement board in the corridor of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what other announcements did you see there, in addition to this one?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among others, there was the decision appointing me into the commission, the decision whereby Hamed Alic ran the communications and information service, and so on. I cannot recall all the decisions. These are the ones I remember. All the decisions adopted would be appended on the board.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was this board -- where was this board located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in the corridor of the municipal building, but it was downstairs, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you see any orders regarding the OS Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you said you attended meetings where Mr. Jusufovic was present and Mr. Halilovic, as well as Mr. Bogilovic, and you handed in reports. Did you review the reports handed in by Mirzet Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what did those reports say?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the reports, but I did not read anybody else's reports. After all, it was not within my possibility to read anybody else's reports. I would hand in my reports and take any assignments or orders that were there for me. I did not linger there. I was not a politician or a member of the War Presidency. I was an operative member of staff who had to act upon the orders given. Therefore, I did not read reports from either the civilian or the military police, or the ones submitted by Hamed Alic. They were not within my reach.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to being the commander of the military police, did Mirzet Halilovic engage in any other function during 1992 or into 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1992, I saw him at Pale, where he had his own self-organised group of fighters. I don't know about any other functions he may have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the group of fighters that he had in Pale, do you remember how many men this included?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was there, I believe he had 20 to 25 men in his group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And he was the leader of the group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after he was called to Srebrenica to be appointed the commander of the military police, did this group continue to exist, the group of men from Pale? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that I know nothing about the later developments, because I went over to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you don't know if this group continued to exist and whether or not there was another leader or whether they engaged in fighting in the Srebrenica, Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that I do not know what happened to the group later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you attend any War Presidency meetings during the time that you were in Srebrenica, 1992 and 1993 specifically?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was not a member of the War Presidency. Only sometimes, if there was an order of the president of the War Presidency to film a meeting, I would go over there -- rather, I wouldn't go there myself; instead, our cameraman, Sabahudin Gluhic, would go there. They didn't even need Vranjkovina to go over there. They only needed the cameraman, Gluhic, to film the meeting, according to the president's orders. He would simply say, "We need a cameraman tomorrow," and we would act upon his order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that the War Presidency did have meetings.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But quite rarely, because of the situation on the ground. And, as I've already indicated, that when there was need for a meeting to be filmed, the president would issue an order accordingly. The meetings could not be held as per normal, because the circumstances did not permit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that you were not a member of the War Presidency, and you just testified that you were not invited, it's a likelihood, is it not, that there were meetings of the War Presidency that you were not aware of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Surely firstly that's an invitation to speculation, since he said that he didn't attend such meetings, and particularly when it's put that there was a likelihood that there were meetings of which he was unaware. That's obviously going to be an invitation for him to speculate about something he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness has testified that -- about the lack of meetings. So -- and he's also testified that he was not present on a number of other occasions. So I think logic dictates that there could have been meetings held outside of his presence that he did not know of, and I think that's a fair question to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Go ahead. Could you please repeat the question. The important thing is, Mr. Sacirovic, that you do not speculate. You just answer the question if you are in a position to answer it. If you're not aware of any such other meetings, then you are to tell us, "I'm not aware of any such other meetings." Otherwise, if you are aware, more or less you give us an indication of what your knowledge consists of, but not beyond that. I will read out Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. At no time did I wish to speculate. I simply want to tell the truth. I am aware of the fact that I have given a solemn oath. I only wish to clarify matters to you, Your Honours, the OTP, and the Defence, and to present the actual truth of what had happened in Srebrenica. And at all times, I wish to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. give accurate and truthful answers, without distinguishing between the sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do not doubt that at any moment, Mr. Sacirovic. Now, the question that Ms. Richardson is putting to you is the following: You have told us of your knowledge about some meetings of the War Presidency for which your troop were invited to film part of the proceedings. So those meetings you are aware of. Are you aware also of other meetings of the War Presidency that you or your group were not invited to, but which you are still aware of as having taken place? If you are, could you give us an indication of where we stand, how many of such meetings of the War Presidency. This is basically what Ms. Richardson is trying to seek from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, distinguished ladies and gentlemen from the Defence and the OTP, I knew only of those meetings for which the president would issue us an order to send a cameraman over. There were only several such meetings. For the rest, I did not know whether or when they took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to pursue the matter any further?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour, that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- You may, of course, but I don't think it's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case of moving to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, were you aware of whether or not the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Avdic, met with members of the armed forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that. I was not even aware of any armed forces. I was only aware of armed groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you came to Srebrenica in June, I believe, of 1992, were you aware that there were different Territorial Defence groups from the various areas who had been put under the command of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not arrive in Srebrenica in June. I arrived in early July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, I do know that Hakija Meholjic had a group, that Akif Ustic had a group, and that almost every village had its own self-organised group. I was not able to meet with all these people and groups at once. I got to know them gradually, as I received assignments and went out into the field. But there were organised groups, as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Richardson, because he hasn't answered your question completely, at least. The question that Ms. Richardson asked you, Mr. Sacirovic, had two matters to be addressed. One was whether you were aware that there were different Territorial Defence groups from various areas, and I think more or less you have answered that. But Ms. Richardson also, in her question, had qualified these different Territorial Defence groups from various areas as being the ones that had been put under the command of Naser Oric, and that part of the question you did not answer. So I repeat the question: You are aware of the existence of a number of Territorial Defence groups from various areas. Are you aware also that these had been put at any time under the command of Naser Oric, but when you first arrived in July of 1992 in Srebrenica? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And the witness certainly didn't accept the existence of a number of Territorial Defence groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He was very specific that it was armed groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I grant you that, certainly, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then if Ms. Richardson wishes to put to him that they were under the command of Naser Oric, that's fine. He did answer these questions in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but she has put her --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a question he's already answered in examination-in-chief. But if she wishes to put it directly, then fine, but let's have the case being put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is also related to the time of his arrival in Srebrenica. So when you first arrived in Srebrenica in July of 1992, were you aware of the existence of groups from various areas having been put under the command of Naser Oric or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, not a single group was under the command of Naser Oric except for a group of 20 to 30 fighters who were with Naser. Not a single group was under Naser Oric's command in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Richardson. And thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, just getting back, just briefly, to the bulletin board you said existed in the municipal building. Did that bulletin board list the members of the War Presidency, and if so, did it list Naser Oric as a member of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a little bit vague and it's because of the way you put the question. It's not the witness's fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think you ought to, because one question is whether on the bulletin board there was ever posted the list of members of the War Presidency. And secondly, if there was, and you're tying it up to the existence of this notice, did the name of Naser Oric appear on it as a member of the War Presidency. So I think there are two questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There are two questions, and I'll separate them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't know which one he answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. Which is always the problem when you put more than one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: First, Mr. Sacirovic, did you see on the bulletin board a notice or a document indicating the members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And therefore the second part --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Indeed. And I'm not sure what time the break will be today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it is convenient for you. We will break now, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, before the break, we were discussing -- you were giving evidence about having seen an order from the War Presidency in the municipal building, and I asked whether or not you had seen an order where Naser Oric was appointed to the War Presidency, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution's Exhibit 42. 42E, I have it as.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not on my list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is on Sanction, and I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but I just remark that it's not on my list; that's all. It would be on other lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the Defence used is it, but I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I can't remember myself, but it is on Sanction and I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it was used as the third document by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it is on Sanction now. I believe we have if now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are seeing, but I want to know what the witness is seeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Sacirovic, having seen this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it in his language, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I just have two questions for you with respect to this document. As you look at article number 4, do you see the name Naser Oric there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it does state that he has been appointed a member of the War Presidency, does it not, along with the other individuals listed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned already to us that you knew Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. Did you know Hamdija Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And were you aware of his position on the War Presidency, as stated here, that he was the executive -- he was the chairman of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Resid Efendic, and I don't want to belabour the point: Did you know him and did he actually work as the secretary of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him very vaguely. I knew him only a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fair enough. And of course you mentioned Becir Bogilovic. Did you also know Jusuf Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it states that he was the commander of the civilian protection staff. Do you recall that being his role?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Mr. Bogilovic, it states under Article 10, that's page 2 of the English, that he was appointed the chief of the public security station. Now, and this document on its face speaks for itself, but there's no information here, just for the record, that he is also the commander of the military police and the civilian police. It just simply states, if you agree with me, that he's the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 10, it says that Becir Bogilovic is appointed chief of the public security service. The civilian and military police fell within its competence. The word "chief" means that he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand, but that's not in this document, is it, what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's telling you that it is implied, basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just establishing for the record that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Okay. Your Honour, I have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think it's clear, what he's telling you. He agrees with you, but he's also telling you that basically the public security service, that's how it was translated to us, not station, covered both, according to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the information you gave us about the fact that the civilian - excuse me - the public security service covered both civilian and military police, where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that because when I handed in my reports to Mr. Hajrudin Avdic, I saw Becir on occasion handing in his reports, and that's when I saw that he was competent to hand in reports for both the civilian and the military police. In his absence, Commander Nurija Jusufovic brought in reports concerning the civilian police, and Mirzet Halilovic did the same for the military police. And these were the two branches falling within the competence of Becir Bogilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So that -- so that we all understand your testimony: It's that because he handed in the reports for Mirzet Halilovic and the -- and Mr. Jusufovic, that this was why you assumed that he was the person over the military and the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, that's not a reason; that's a fact. Becir Bogilovic was the superior of Becir Bogilovic [as interpreted] and Nurija Jusufovic. He was their chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You didn't see this on any documents anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Mirzet Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that in the document. I know that from practice. I knew that from the situation. Because I was there in Srebrenica. I was in the municipal building. I was present during conversations. And I can assert with certainty that Becir Bogilovic was the superior of both Mirzet Halilovic and Nurija Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I take it that prior to your being made president of the commission, prior to the war, you had not worked with or been a member of the War Presidency in the past, had you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither before nor after.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So whatever information you have is not based on your -- I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm actually finished with that document. If Madam Usher could remove it from the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified that Mr. Naser Oric -- that the groups, in fact, had not -- were all independent and they were not organised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every group was self-organised and they were not under the command of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd like Prosecution's Exhibit 73 be put to the witness, and I will also be using 74 and Prosecution's Exhibit 4E as well. So the first document to be shown to the witness is Prosecution's Exhibit 73, and it will be on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, if you just look at this document, it's dated May 20th. It's from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica Territorial Staff. There is a decision, the Srebrenica municipal TO staff is hereby formed. Now, I would just like to ask you first: On May 20th - excuse me - I'll rephrase. Were you aware that on May 20th the Srebrenica municipal TO staff had been formed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Reading further, the following -- under II: "The following shall be appointed to the Srebrenica TO staff." It lists Naser Oric from Potocari, as Commander of the Srebrenica TO staff. It also goes on to list Akif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Hamdija Fejzic, Sevket Dzozic, Becir Bogilovic, and Ahmo Tihic. Now, I believe you testified that you know Zulfo Tursunovic, you know Becir Bogilovic, and of course you know Ahmo Tihic. You testified that you also know Hamdija Fejzic. Did you know Sevket Dzozic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Akif Ustic, he was from Srebrenica, and he had a group of his own, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you also testified that that's the same for Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Hamdija Fejzic, were you aware whether or not he was a member of the Bajramovici group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know if he was from Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And on the second page, it states, under III: "The decision shall enter into force on the day of its adoption." I won't belabour all of the information. But the very last sentence reads, and I'll just go down to the last two lines: "A single military command of all armed groups shall be formed under the name of Srebrenica TO," and it is signed by the Commander, Srebrenica TO staff. And the word "Naser" appears, and there's a stamp on the original. There is a recording clerk, who is Hamdija Fejzic. Were you aware that Naser Oric had been made commander of the Srebrenica TO staff, including all of these other groups?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could show the witness P74. This document, for the record, is also dated the 20th of May, Bajramovici, 1992, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica TO territorial staff. It says "a decision." Decision, under I, Becir Bogilovic, from Srebrenica, a policeman, the former commander of the Srebrenica SJB public security station, is appointed temporary police commander in the town of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, first off, did you know about this decision from, specifically, the territorial staff, involving Mr. Bogilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, to what's -- I'll rephrase. Under the statement of reasons, I will go down to the -- three lines from the paragraph itself. It says that: "Bogilovic shall be temporarily accountable for his work to the Srebrenica TO staff to the above bodies once they have been set up, and to the authorised institutions in Tuzla and Sarajevo when they too have been set up." So were you aware that he, Mr. Bogilovic, would be accountable to the TO staff in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you the next document, Prosecution's Exhibit 4E. For the record, it is Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica TO, Srebrenica, the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 4E. E to me means English, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I could --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I should write E and I'm repeating what I see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could live with that. It saves me having to try and understand Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to make sure that the witness is being shown something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. And the witness should be shown ERN 01239504.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I will read the order itself, which is signed by Naser and there's a stamp on the original. It says "Commander Srebrenica TO. With the aim of confronting the aggressor and engaging in a struggle for liberation" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Do we have it on Sanction or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We're working on it, Your Honour. I'll take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you can start reading, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Okay

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "All" -- "With the aim of confronting the aggressor and engaging in the struggle for liberation, all the local leaders of self-organised armed groups are ordered to immediately commence developing the organisation and establishment of the Srebrenica TO units, in particular...", and then it lists: "Srebrenica" TO to be organised by Naser Oric, Potocari, Suceska, Omasce TO," et cetera.
