And I would draw your attention to number 10. "Services to be attached to Srebrenica TO." Do you see that? Under A it says "war hospital to be set up by Avdo Hasanovic."

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you spent a lot of time in the hospital. Was Mr. Avdo Huseinovic the head of the hospital or the director of the Srebrenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But he was working in the hospital, was he not, one of the doctors?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did work in the hospital. I don't know about him being some kind of head or chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Now, under number -- under B it says: "Signals and information service to be set up by Hamed Halilovic." Thank you. Hamid Alic, Your Honour. I stand corrected. Were you aware that the Srebrenica TO established a signals and information set-up information service which was head up -- or set up by Hamed Alic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. On my arrival from Pale to Srebrenica, in July, I found Hamed Alic already performing that duty. The rest I'm not aware of, who appointed him or when. That I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But you were aware that he worked for the War Presidency, but you were not aware that he was also part of the Srebrenica TO, as a member, who would be heading up the signals and information service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, C --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The interpretation is still going. I heard the witness saying yes while the interpretation is still going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing that out. Let's make sure that we've got it all right. I will repeat to you the question, please, Mr. Sacirovic, and then you answer slowly, and make sure that first the interpretation exercise has come to an end. "But you were aware," asked -- said Ms. Richardson, "that he worked for the War Presidency, but you were not aware that he was also part of the Srebrenica TO, as a member, who would be heading up the signals and information service?" And we are, of course, talking about Hamed Alic. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware that Hamed Alic worked for the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality. I'm not, however, aware of him working for some kind of Territorial Defence Staff of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson. Is that all right with both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed. And with respect to C, at the VP, which is the military -- abbreviation for military police, firing positions, that's what it says in English, the organisation to be carried out by Mirzet Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, based on what you previously told us, that Mirzet Halilovic was the chief of police, did you know that he was also a member or part of the Srebrenica TO and elected to be someone who would organise the military police?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here under C is "VP." I believe that's some kind of military police. I'm not, however, aware of Mirzet Halilovic being included in the Srebrenica TO. I do know that he was appointed commander of the military police by the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any questions on that document. Madam Usher can take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance again in showing document P79. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, just for the record, this document is from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, operations staff of the armed forces, Srebrenica. It is dated Srebrenica, 19th September, 1992. It is to the War Presidency of the municipality. And the subject matter is draft decision regarding the set-up of departments and appointing chiefs of these departments in the operations staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I have already reacted by asking that the translation of this document be corrected. It should be placed on the ELMO, because in the Bosnian version, it states "proposal," whereas in the English version it is "draft decision." The word "proposal" has nothing to do with the English translation of the -- as it states here, "draft decision," and I would kindly ask the interpreters to confirm this. I've already drawn attention of the Prosecutor to this, but they have not corrected it. Your Honours, it substantially changes the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to discuss this in the presence of the witness or in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm short on time today, and perhaps we can just place it on the ELMO. We can revisit the issue when we have more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In any case, he's going to see the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And keep in mind what has been suggested by Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically we're talking of a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I believe the English will be on Sanction in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, under number 8, you see the name Hamed Alic, and it's the department for communication. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the -- you're not aware, Mr. Sacirovic, whether or not the Srebrenica War Presidency had to approve these members as submitted here of the Operations Staff of the Armed Forces, are you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions. Thank you, Madam Usher, for placing this document. If I could just have a moment. At this time I would like the witness to be shown Prosecution's Exhibit P84. Sorry. We will be, for the English, we will be referring to ERN 03090721. Just a moment, Your Honour. And for the B/C/S, ERN 02115063. At least that's the beginning portion. And it should start with the date November 3rd, 1992, meeting of the Armed Forces Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it will be easier if you gave us the page number in the English version, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll do so right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but we have been seeing different pages on Sanction, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But on Sanction we have the 7th November, and you said the 3rd November, if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's the 3rd of November. So we need to go forward one page on Sanction. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the previous page, page 16 we need to see. And then it's another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could see -- I could see it referring --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The date is at the very bottom, last page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So now, Mr. Sacirovic, I hope everyone has it now and can follow. Do you see the date 3rd November, meeting of the Armed Forces Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, it does state that -- well, first I should ask you: Have you ever attended any meetings of the Armed Forces Staff of Srebrenica during your time there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, let me refer you to a portion of this page, which talks about the work of communication and information service. The sentence reads, at least in English: "As for the work of the communication and information service," and you may need to turn to the next page, ERN 02115064, because ... It states: "In fact, it consists" and I'll wait until you can see it. It says -- on the previous page, it says: "As for the work of the communication and information service," and then it states: "In fact, it consists of two services, the communication service operating within the Armed Forces, and the information service." Something that's illegible. "It is believed that a special commission of the War Presidency must be formed for the communication and information service for information regarding war destruction..." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let him -- we just want to know whether -- because we've been waiting for you to say whether you can see it on that page or not, whether you've read it or not. Have you found it or not yet? It's at the top of the page. That page has a number, which is 02115064. And this is at the very top of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, I'm sorry I cut you off, but I wanted to make sure that he had the right page in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will get back to this in our re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, your question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm moving, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this information here, you testified yesterday that -- and you were shown Defence Exhibit 862, that in fact a document which was signed by -- a document -- I'll rephrase the question. Yesterday you were asked about whether or not Nijaz Masic had been approved or appointed by the communication and information service for -- and that his work involved collecting information about genocide perpetrated by the occupiers against Muslims, Croats, and other ethnic groups. I'm just paraphrasing from the document. But do you recall seeing that document?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, this is the first time I see this document, and I repeat that I am not aware of Nijaz Masic's role, as I indicated earlier in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think he has misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, and I will show him the document with what he's looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the document that we showed you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: [Speakers overlapping: Cannot distinguish between speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- yesterday or the day before. You remember we showed you a document in which it was stated that Nijaz Masic was being appointed to conduct investigations on genocide. Do you remember that? And you told us that you didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I'm stating right now. I truly don't know anything about it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was about that document. I mean, do you remember seeing that document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was actually Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. On Monday. It was Monday, in fact, because I referred to it yesterday, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do recall seeing the document, but I am not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move to another subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If the usher could render her assistance again and show the witness, with the same Prosecution exhibit, page ERN 02115071. And for -- in the English version I believe it's ERN 03090726. And we'll bring it up on the ELMO. I believe it's page 21. If we could put the section that states -- the portion that begins right -- that -- the first sentence is: "The military police belong to the Armed Forces and not the War Presidency." So it's ERN 02115071.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the previous page, the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The English is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, you said that you've never attended meetings, and I take it also you are not aware of whether or not the -- you testified previously -- let me rephrase. You testified previously that you were not aware of whether or not Mr. Alic met with the OS Staff and had any meetings with them. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Right. Now, just for the record, and you don't need to turn to this, but the meeting is dated 9 November 1992. It says: "Minutes of the joint meeting of the War Presidency and the Srebrenica Armed Forces." And it is ERN 03090723. And the B/C/S is 02115068. I don't need that to be shown the witness, but I'd like you to look at the page that's before you. Now, were you aware that there was a discussion held and it was stated in the meeting that the military police belonged to the Armed Forces and not the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. And I know exactly what you're going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it's a fair question for the witness, unless he's aware that this is the note of what one person appears to have said. When it's put that way, that this was stated at the meeting, it's as if it were the consensus of the whole meeting or that it was agreed upon. He has a right to see in context that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree 100 per cent with you. I think you have to put to the witness that there is one individual who is stated five, six lines above -- actually, it's on the previous page, and it's that individual who is making this statement, Zulfo, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe I said it was stated. So I will rephrase the question and say one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it was stated, in other words, it can have a completely different connotation. I mean, that's why I'm agreeing with Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Sacirovic, in this -- in the minutes of this meeting that we're reviewing, it is stated by the last person, and that is indicated on 03090725, and of the B/C/S it's 02115070, and it's stated by Zulfo: "We have past regulation until freedom is achieved. Let us punish" a word is crossed out, "offenders. The court cannot pass final judgement. It has not been formed properly as it is a preventive task." And then he goes on to say: "The military police belong to the Armed Forces." And it goes on to say, the next line, that: "The military police belong to the Armed Forces and not to the War Presidency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it has to do with translation. I'm not sure if this -- what the Prosecutor said was interpreted properly, but it seems as if Zulfo had said, "We had received rules for the internal police," whereas it says here Zulfo says that he -- the rules ought to be passed, need to be passed, whereas through interpretation into Bosnian, it seemed as if the rules for the military police had been adopted. Could the witness please look at the document. Either the Prosecutor misspoke when she was reading or the interpretation was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. The Prosecutor was reading correctly. It's maybe a question of misinterpretation. However, the witness has got the text in B/C/S, the original text in B/C/S, and he can read it for himself. And it is obvious from it that there is no indication that a decision had already been taken, or regulations had already been passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, and my question, Your Honour, is specifically with respect to that one sentence, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- what comes before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So my question, Mr. Sacirovic: Had you heard or learned that the military police indeed reported to or belonged to the Armed Forces and not the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I have never heard this. The military police was exclusively subordinated to the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, if an order existed that was signed by Naser Oric ordering the military police, would that - the fact that he, Naser Oric, has issued an order to the military police - change your position?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, Naser Oric could not have issued an order changing any titles. I repeat: The military police was subordinated to the president of the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, and Naser Oric could not have played any role in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you look further down, under the same page, I believe it's still on the same page, under "information," it has Hamed, and from that name, it is stated: "We have collected much information. So far we have sent 120 reports. Until mid-September, we worked both for the military police - excuse me - military and the civilian authorities. We have to procure oil and generator parts ourselves. Communication and information must be separated." Now, again, I believe you previously testified that you were not aware that the information Hamed Alic worked both for the War Presidency and the Armed Forces. Now, based on a reading of what's stated in the minute, is it now clear to you that indeed Hamed Alic reported both to the military and the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, as far as I know, Hamed Alic reported -- or rather, submitted his reports only to the War Presidency, and not to any armed forces, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So but having read what's in the minutes, does this change your position, that there is a possibility, at the very least, that he reported both to the Armed Forces and to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This does not change my position at all. I categorically state that Hamed Alic submitted his reports exclusively to the War Presidency of Srebrenica municipality, or to be more precise, to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Mr. Hamed Alic about whether he submitted any official reports to the Armed Forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never heard Hamed Alic utter the words "Armed Forces," let alone -- or rather, and I only saw him submitting reports to the president of the War Presidency, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part that he stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sacirovic, the interpreters couldn't catch up with you, the final part of your testimony. You said: "I had never heard Hamed Alic utter the words Armed Forces, let alone, or rather, and I only saw him submitting reports to the president of the War Presidency." And then you said something else, but the interpreters didn't catch it. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that Hamed Alic was subordinated to and submitted his reports solely to the War Presidency, that's to say, Mr. Hajrudin Avdic. That was what I stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So in response to my question, the answer is no, Mr. Hamed Alic never spoke to you about submitting reports to the Armed Forces of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, I am not aware at all that there were Armed Forces of Srebrenica in existence at the time. I only know that there were armed groups around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, further down the page, it says "commission." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And just before that, Nijaz Masic states: "For the first two and a half months the service worked well. Now a new man has to be appointed - information. Likewise, a commission for collecting and processing information on war casualties must be formed." And then it goes on, commission, and there are five names listed. It says Becir, Masic, Osman, Avdo, Fadil. Do you see that? It should probably be at the end of your page, the B/C/S, list of five names.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified that -- well, you were shown Defence Exhibit 263. And perhaps we can show the witness this document again. Now, if you look at Roman numeral -- well, I should first read into the record what this document is titled. "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica municipality, War Presidency, Srebrenica, 12 November, 1992." It states: "A War Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality at a meeting held on the 9th November 1992 adopted the following decision." It says: "Decision on the establishment of a commission." I: "A commission is to be formed of the follow composition: Nijaz Masic, Avdo Huseinovic, Fadil Mujic [phoen]," and it lists Nijaz Masic as the chair and the other two as member. Now, having read the minutes of -- the joint minutes that I just read to you about the commission, does the information from the minutes and this decision, are they not very similar, in that it appears as though this is an order that came out of the commission that was proposed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you that I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions on that document. Perhaps you can keep P484 -- P84, excuse me, with the witness. I do have some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, just to complete a series of questions from this document. You previously testified that Mirzet Halilovic was the commander of the military police and that at one point he was removed and he was replaced by Atif Krzic. Do you remember your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance in showing the ERN page, B/C/S firstly, 02115077. And in the English, 030907 -- 0. It's possibly found on page 25 or 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, and also to help us, what's the exact --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- ERN number in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In English it's 03090730.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it's the meeting is dated -- the minutes, minutes of the Srebrenica OS Staff meeting held on the 22nd of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. It is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to take a look at number 5. It says: "Miscellaneous: Reorganisation of the VP," which is abbreviation for the military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do need the usher's assistance again. I apologise. But I need the witness to be shown ERN 02115079, which is a couple of pages after the document he's shown. And for the English it's 03097033.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, do you see the name Mirzet Halilovic, resignation, unanimously accepted?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see some things and I don't see some other things, because these documents are not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's perhaps start with the name. Do you see the name Mirzet Halilovic? It's probably towards the middle portion of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you see the Roman numerals VI? It's three lines above that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Having located the name, it says: "Resignation unanimously accepted." And the second line states: "K Atif unanimously, one against, one abstained." Now, having read this, is this consistent with what you told us, that Mirzet Halilovic was replaced as the chief of military police, command of the military police, and he was replaced by Atif Kurtic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Kurtic. Krgic. [phoen]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you so much, yes. And is that correct, he was replaced by Mr. Krgic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirzet Halilovic was replaced, but the usual procedure anywhere in the world, if somebody makes a mistake, whether a politician or any kind of official, it's suggested to that person that he should resign.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like this document to remain with the witness, and I would like the witness to be shown document -- Prosecution's Exhibit 14, P14.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And Mr. Sacirovic, I do need for the record your answer to my questions that Krgic replaced Mirzet Halilovic, a simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, before you review the document that's being placed before you, Mr. Sacirovic, if you could just -- could I have your attention, please. I'd like to ask you a question before you review that document. My question is whether you were aware that Naser Oric was also meeting with members of the War Presidency, including Mr. Hajrudin Avdic.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you stated that the War Presidency was the highest organ in Srebrenica. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the document that's before you, and just for the record, I will read what's stated in this document. "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica Armed Forces Staff, Srebrenica, the 22nd of December, 1992." And it's to the president of the War Presidency. And it states: "Further to a conclusion adopted at a meeting of the Srebrenica OS Staff on the 22nd of December, 1992, the Srebrenica OS Staff issues the following order: To convene a session of the War Presidency and the Srebrenica OS Staff on the 23rd of December at 10.00, 1000 hours. The president of the War Presidency shall be duty-bound to ensure a quorum for the meeting by the beginning of the meeting at the appointed time." And it is signed Commander Naser Oric, commander of the Srebrenica OS. Now, having read this document, does it appear to you that Mr. Oric himself ordered -- sent an order to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This document does not state that this is an order sent to the War Presidency from Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was Naser to send an order to the president of the War Presidency? I don't believe this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. utterances.text: All right. Further in the document, it says: "As soon as the war broke out, the Chetnik issued an ultimatum on the 17th of April, 1992, that we lay down our weapons and with his group he went to Pale, where he was chosen to be company commander." Now, you told us before he was in Pale and that he was the leader of a group. Would that be correct? Is that similar to what you know of him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, it also states that he took part in the sabotage action in Potocari against Arkan's men. And I believe you testified that Naser Oric was also -- or was involved in the sabotage of Arkan's men. Do you know if Mr. Mirzet Halilovic was also involved?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And further down on the page, it says: "From the 4th of July, 1992, he was the military police commander." And I believe you already told us when you arrived in Srebrenica, Mirzet was also contacted to become the military police commander.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the military police in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And it also states that he took, he, meaning Mirzet Halilovic, took part in major combat actions such as those at Brezani, Fakovici, Provranje [phoen] and the liberation of Sase, Bjelovac, Olavica [phoen]. Do you know if he took part in any of the various battles or action, combat actions listed here?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But these battles did take place? You are aware that these actions did take place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were actions of defence. I am not aware of any offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it says further down: "During his service in the police, he was permanently exposed to danger because in addition to -- because in addition to performing the task in the town itself, he and his combatants had to be on the front line too at any time, day or night, to perform the assigned task. He had travelled sometimes as far as 20 kilometres or further to our front line in Purica Brdo [phoen], or the line in Suceska. And he had to perform his task in a good and correct manner." Are you familiar with whether or not -- well, it does say that he performed his task in town, so do you agree that part of his task as a military commander, military police commander, that he had various tasks to perform in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is not quite clear to me. I know that he had tasks within Srebrenica. I am not aware of him performing any tasks outside Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. So you're not aware of whether or not he was present at the front line engaged as a fighter?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And towards the end, it states that a big and crucial battle for him occurred in the region of Jezero, wherein an assault with several of his fellow men against a stronghold he aimed to destroy he suffered heavy wounds inflicted by a grenade that fell in his vicinity and he died at the spot. Now, is that how Mr. Mirzet Halilovic died, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how Mr. Halilovic got killed. I only heard that he got killed, but I am not aware of the time period or the circumstances surrounding his death.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could have an exhibit number, and I would appreciate it if the usher could remove this document from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson. This document, which consists of one page in B/C/S, bearing ERN 03721052, and the corresponding translation thereof into English, consisting of two pages, is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P951.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacirovic, you testified that you observed and you filmed, or was part of an interview where Serb civilians were in Srebrenica and that they were exchanged. Do you remember that testimony? And we watched a video of you interviewing them.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- where those people were from exactly? I think you said it could have been from Karno.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from the villages to the east of Srebrenica. The village of Karno, that was the information I received during my interview. It's a very small village that cannot be found on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And was it a Muslim - excuse me - was it a Serb village or was it a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a Serb village. But let me tell you, all these villages were mixed. Some had a Muslim majority, others a Serb majority. But for the most part, they were mixed. As for the village of Karno, I am not sure whether it was a Muslim or a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm being advised that there needs to be a correction to the transcript, and it's page 78, line 9, where the exhibit number is entered as 951 and I believe it's 591.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben, and thank you, Ms. Richardson. That's correct. It's being marked as Prosecution exhibit 5 -- P591 and not 951 as is shown on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, do you know how it was these Serb civilians were -- why it was they were taken prisoner and ended up in Srebrenica, in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when they were taken prisoner, why or by whom. I only know that Nurija Jusufovic came to me and told me that the chief had ordered that we should go and film the exchange of prisoners, and that's what you saw on the video footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that was exchanging them, who it was on the Muslim side, and whether or not this person was negotiating with the Serb side? Do you have any information of that nature?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners were taken for exchange by the commander of the civilian police, Nurija Jusufovic. We made this video footage, as ordered by the chief. They were taken further for the exchange, but I don't know whether they were in fact exchanged or where. I completed my part of the job and went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you -- could you tell us if, having lived in -- I believe you were born in Hranca and you lived in Glogova. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you frequently visit the Serbian side, across from the Drina River, to engage in any type of business activity, such as shopping or working or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When? Which period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, as I said, in January 1992, I went to Sabac, bought a gun -- bought a rifle and returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And even -- that wasn't the only time you visited, I take it, during your lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Serbia? Well, before the war I went to Serbia several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And not only you, but the civilian population in your area, Glogova, the villages that are close to the Drina, I take it that people would frequently go to Serbia and people from Serbia would come to the Bosnian side as well.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a free country. People could go wherever they wanted to go. There were people from Bosnia who worked in Serbia. There were people from Serbia who worked in Bosnia or Croatia. All these were republics of the former Yugoslavia. There was freedom of movement for everyone who wanted to move about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So there was an integration of the Muslims from the Bosnian side of the Drina, as well as the Serbs from the Serb side, across? Your lives intermingled?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. And so it would not be an unusual occurrence for a Bosnian, a Bosniak, someone of Muslim ethnicity, from the Bosnian side, to use Serb words, and I take it the same is true, that for a Serb from the Serbian side, it would not be unusual for them to use a Bosniak word or a word used by Muslims, because they had been so integrated over the years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think that question is so vague that the witness couldn't possibly answer. If we're talking about the Ekavian dialect and the Ijekavian dialect, then perhaps the witness can be asked about that, but which words is my learned friend referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, let me say, I don't think counsel should suggest to me what I am asking him about. It is my cross-examination, and I am seeking to elicit from him whether or not there was an intermingling of various phrases or language, and if I would suggest counsel not suggest to the witness where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't suggested. I think it was obvious from your question, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think you should proceed and take it in -- take it in parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So let me ask this, having heard the exchange, Mr. Sacirovic: It wouldn't be unusual, I take it, for the Muslims from the Bosnian side of the Drina to use some Serb words?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina speak the Ijekavian accent, for the most part, whereas in Serbia they use the Ekavian variant, which is why one can always know whether a person comes from across the Drina River, that is, from Serbia, or from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, there is a difference in the language or in the accent, as it were. There was a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I do understand that in general there was a big difference, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm asking if there were phrases or words that the Muslim Bosniaks may have adopted from the Serbs because they had been -- their lives were so integrated.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So it's unheard of for a Muslim from the Bosnian -- a Bosniak village aside of the Drina to ever use a Serb word? Not the entire dialect; a word or a phrase.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the following possibility, if this is a Bosniak Muslim -- a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosniak. Even the Serbs speak the Ijekavian dialect if they were from Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, if a person had been living in Belgrade for 10 or 15 years, then it was only normal for the person to use the Ekavian dialect. I am not aware of any other such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirovic, I would ask you to answer the question that I'm asking. I'm not asking about the dialect in its totality. I'm asking about a word or a phrase from the dialect that a Muslim would adopt because he would have been associating with Serbs for all of his life.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Yes, such phrases were possible. One could not rule that out. But I don't know what you're asking me specifically about. I don't find your question clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I believe you have answered the question. So the answer is yes, that that's -- that was the case, that Muslims would or could use Serb words or phrases because their lives had been so integrated throughout the years?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to you was yes, if the person had spent a longer period of time in Serbia, it was natural for that person to adopt the dialect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. You did answer my question. Now I would like to ask you -- move on to another area and get back to the work of your commission. You testified that the work of your commission also entailed documenting all war crimes, not just those committed by Serbs against Muslims. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And with that in mind, did you visit any -- well, did you hear -- I should ask: Did you hear about crimes committed by Muslims against Serbs during 1992, 1993, and up until the time you left Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So not one person indicated to you -- when I say "person," not any of the Muslims you came in contact indicated to you that crimes were being committed against Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, did you hear about civilians being killed in the actions orchestrated by the Muslims' fighters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When you interviewed the fighters, did they talk to you about the casualties on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't even ask them about it. It simply wasn't my task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk much to the fighters. I was more interested in the civilian population. I wanted to know when and where a crime was committed. It is true that we were collecting information about any crimes committed by any side. However, I simply did not have the opportunity, Madam Prosecutor. I was cut off. I did not have access to the territory to -- eye-witnesses who on the other side who would be able to provide information on a war crime committed by the Muslim side, if any. And I assure you that I would have done my task in that case just as I did for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you visit Kravica in January of 1993, after - thank you - after there had been an action by the Muslim fighters on January 7th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I visited Kravica sometime on the 8th, 9th, or 10th of March, 1993, when the French general Philippe Morillon was about to arrive and we had an order to go to Konjevic Polje on the occasion of his arrival. However, because of the Serbian shelling attack, I came down to Kravica and by the time I reached the centre of Kravica, the shelling started and I ordered my team to return as soon as possible because there were clashes down there. It was dangerous. And that was the only time I spent in Kravica and Glogova. It was later on that I came to Konjevic Polje and Glogova. At that point in time, we were not allowed to go further.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the time that you did visit Kravica and Glogova, these were the periods that it was in the hands of the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's assume -- let assume it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Might as well do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you arrived at these places, even though you didn't -- when I say "places," give an example, Glogova and Kravica, even though you didn't stay long, did you notice that the houses and some of the buildings had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some houses were torched and damaged. That's true. But I went along the asphalt road. I was with my team. There were many people fleeing from Konjevic Polje in the direction of Bratunac and Glogova and were directed to go to Srebrenica. Chaos prevailed already at that time. It was an emergency situation. As I heard the explosions and I saw what was going on, I ordered the members of my team to go back, because it was not safe. And that's how we returned to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you said that houses were torched. Were they -- those houses that you observed that had been torched, was this in Kravica or Glogova? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: The houses in Glogova were razed to the ground, all of them; 100 per cent of them were razed to the ground. As for Kravica, I did not pass through the entire village. I only arrived to the centre, and I saw maybe some dozens of houses. Some of them were singed, a bit burnt; others were not. However, I was not in a position to observe these matters. Had the situation been safe, I would have filmed all of this, including General Morillon's arrival. However, the circumstances prevailing at the time did not permit us to do so, and we had to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So even if -- I'll rephrase the question. When you listened to the radio - you were telling us earlier that you had a transistor radio and would listen to the Serb news, et cetera - did you hear that the Serbs were stating that a number of their civilians had been killed in this region? And by "the region," I mean had been killed in Kravica or had been killed in Glogova or Jezestica during 1992 and 1993, or in Rakovici. Did you hear any of that on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was listening to the radio, and I listened only occasionally, I did not hear the Serb radio broadcasting that information. I did not have occasion to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you were asked -- I just -- one more question with respect to damage to Serb property or killing of Serb civilians. You were shown an exhibit, and I believe it was Exhibit 294. And part of that exhibit included information regarding property damage that had occurred in various areas. And I'm not going to go through all of it right now, but it claimed Jezestica, Kravica, et cetera. So is it your position that you were not in a position to confirm the information about the damage of the homes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to do that. I wasn't there. And if I had no evidence, I can't assert that. It would be wrong. So I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that, again, you didn't speak to anyone in Srebrenica or hear about Serb houses being burned in Jezestica and other areas in the region?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were asked about whether or not you know Kemo. I believe his name is Kemal Mehmedovic, and I probably didn't pronounce it correctly. Do you recall that testimony when you were asked by Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that. He asked me about Kemal Mehmedovic. There are many people nicknamed Kemo but I do know Kemal Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you know him from Pale, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He hails from Pale, and I spent almost two months there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during the two months that you were in Pale, did you -- did you come in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would see each other occasionally, but we weren't really close friends. I'm acquainted with the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And during that period of time, do you know if he was part of any of the fighting groups that you've discussed, perhaps under Mirzet Halilovic, or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, he did not belong to any group. They had a tractor, they had horses, and he and his father worked in the village. I didn't observe him belonging to any armed group in the area during the time I was in Pale. As for later, when I went to Srebrenica, I don't know where he went or what he did, or anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And while in Srebrenica, did you happen to hear of a story involving Kemo where he was carrying around the head of a Serb individual?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This was the first time you've heard of it today in this courtroom or did you hear of it after the war?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time, now, in the courtroom, that I've heard about Kemo carrying around a head.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would -- just one other question with respect to the military police. Did you -- you said you knew Mirzet Halilovic and he had other policemen under him. Did you talk to those other policemen at any point in time during the time that you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my previous testimony, I have already said I didn't know these men and they were not in uniform, so it was hard to identify them. I only knew Mirzet Halilovic, and the reason I knew him was that I would come across him in the building of the Srebrenica municipality, when he came to report to the War Presidency president, Mr. Avdic. As for the rest, it did not fall within the domain of my office. And Srebrenica was overcrowded, and you couldn't tell who was who.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Of course. Now, when you testified previously about the Serb civilians being exchanged, did you have occasion to visit the prison in Srebrenica, either the police station, where there was detention cells, or the other prison? Did you know that there were Serb prisoners being held there in perhaps October or in January and February of 1993? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. The only prisoners I knew existed in Srebrenica were the ones I interviewed. Nurija Jusufovic, the commander of the civilian police, came to me and said, "The president of the War Presidency has ordered that we go and film those civilian prisoners of war." They were people who were poor, poor people, in a miserable state. I went and I filmed them, and that was all. As for others, for the first time I have heard this, and I cannot tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction. The witness did say "poor people." He did not say -- he did not use those other words, "in a miserable condition." I don't think the interpreters should add to what the witness said. He only said "poor people."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say poor people, because we were all poor people. When you look at the tape, they were no different from me or the rest of us. You saw how thin we all were. We were all poor, all in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I'm informed that we definitely have to stop at 1345 because this courtroom is needed by another team for other purposes at 1350.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not be done, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we will --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified you didn't know about the Serb prisoners. Did you hear any rumours in Srebrenica that prisoners were being held there, other than the ones that you observed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, had I heard about it, I would have done whatever was within my ability to do. I didn't even know about these prisoners that I interviewed until Nurija Jusufovic came and told me that the president of the War Presidency had ordered that we go and film them. I didn't know about any other prisoners apart from the ones I interviewed. I didn't know any other prisoners existed in Srebrenica. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So when is the first time you heard that there were other Serb prisoners in Srebrenica? Is it only as you arrived in the Tribunal this week, or did you hear about this at some later date -- some earlier date, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard there were other Serb prisoners in Srebrenica, apart from the group I interviewed. It's only here in The Hague that I've heard, and I've heard it from you, that there were other Serb prisoners in Srebrenica. I don't know of any others, apart from the ones I interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So would you be surprised to learn that there are Serb prisoners -- that there were Serb prisoners and that they were beaten while they were held in detention in Srebrenica and that perhaps some may have died there? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a person, I would have been surprised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you had contact with Hamed Salihovic. Or I should say: Did you have contact with Hamed Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have contact with Hamed Salihovic in 1994, while I was secretary of the War Presidency of Bratunac municipality. At the time, Hamed Salihovic was a president of some kind of subregion on paper, and we would discuss whether this subregion of Vlasenica, Bratunac, Zvornik, Srebrenica, could come to life, start functioning. But I assert with full responsibility that this was not possible. It could never begin functioning because of the situation we were in, the occupation, the daily shelling, the fact that people were being killed on a daily basis. Hamed Salihovic, at that time, was the most influential political figure in the area, and that's what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, were you aware of what type of role or the various tasks Mr. Hamed Salihovic had in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not aware of any other role of Hamed Salihovic during the war, up until 1994. When I met him in 1994, in the office of the president of the War Presidency of Bratunac municipality, he told me that before the war he had worked in the Srebrenica public security service. That's when I got to know him a bit better. The CSB. Before that, I didn't know Hamed Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And did he talk to you about the fact that -- well, I'll rephrase. And you don't know whether or not he was involved with the prisoners in Srebrenica in August -- in October of 1992 or into 1993? You wouldn't know that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In fact, you weren't even aware that there were prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA SACIROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I didn't know there were any other prisoners, or any prisoners at all, until Nurija came and told me to film those people who were going to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is an opportune time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Richardson. Mr. Sacirovic, we have to stop here, because our time is over and this courtroom is needed by another Trial Chamber. We will continue and finish tomorrow morning. You won't be here for long. And I think the VW section can proceed with the preparations to repatriate the witness, at the earliest possible opportunity. So I thank you, and we'll meet again tomorrow. Tomorrow I am having a sitting myself at 8.00, separate from this case, and I hope to finish by 9.00. I hope -- I'll make an effort to finish by 9.00, but it's the Seselj case. It doesn't make a difference if it's this courtroom or another courtroom. The question is: I don't know for sure that I will manage to finish by 9.00. But I will make a big effort to finish by 9.00 so that we can then start immediately after and finish with this witness. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of November, 2005, at 1.46 p.m.
